Reference: Lee (2008)

Model Setting

The paper asks when a regression-discontinuity design (RDD) delivers causal inferences as credible as those from a randomized experiment, even though individuals can influence the score that determines treatment. Hahn, Todd and van der Klaauw (2001) show that the sharp RDD identifies a treatment effect if E[Y0∣V=v]E[Y_0|V=v]E[Y0​∣V=v] and E[Y1∣V=v]E[Y_1|V=v]E[Y1​∣V=v] are continuous in vvv at the threshold v0v_0v0​, where Y1Y_1Y1​ and Y0Y_0Y0​ are the potential outcomes and VVV is the score. For the applied researcher this assumption has two limitations. It is not a description of a treatment-assigning process but a statement of what must be mathematically true if the RD gap is causal, so its plausibility is hard to judge when individuals have some influence over their score. It is also fundamentally untestable.

The paper replaces it with a description of the assignment mechanism. Each individual has a score VVV that depends on his or her attributes and actions and on random chance; treatment is given if and only if VVV crosses a known threshold. The single substantive assumption is that, conditional on the individual's characteristics and choices, the density of VVV is continuous, while that density may differ arbitrarily across individuals. Under this condition of imprecise control over the score, treatment status is as good as randomized in a neighbourhood of the threshold: the distribution of unobserved types is the same just above and just below it, the discontinuity in the conditional mean of the outcome is a weighted average treatment effect, and every variable determined before assignment is balanced at the threshold. The last property is a testable implication, exactly as baseline balance is in a randomized trial. The idea is applied to elections to the U.S. House of Representatives from 1946 to 1998. Districts where the Democrats barely won and barely lost are similar in all pre-determined characteristics, and winning raises the party's vote share in the next election by about 0.08 and its probability of winning the next election by about 0.35 to 0.45 depending on the outcome definition; losing lowers the probability that the candidate runs again by about 0.40 to 0.43.

Classical Randomized Experiment

The benchmark is the mechanism that draws an individual at random from a population, assigns treatment with a constant probability p0p_0p0​, and then measures all variables. The observables are (Y,X,D)(Y,X,D)(Y,X,D): the outcome YYY, a pre-determined variable XXX whose value is fixed before assignment, and the treatment indicator DDD. Only one potential outcome is observed:

Y=DY1+(1−D)Y0(1)Y=DY_1+(1-D)Y_0 \tag{1}Y=DY1​+(1−D)Y0​(1)

To separate the draw of the individual from the assignment of treatment, Condition 1a introduces an unobservable random variable WWW, the type or identity of the individual, and makes all potential outcomes and baseline variables functions of it:

Y1≡y1(W),Y0≡y0(W),X≡x(W)(2)Y_1\equiv y_1(W),\qquad Y_0\equiv y_0(W),\qquad X\equiv x(W) \tag{2}Y1​≡y1​(W),Y0​≡y0​(W),X≡x(W)(2)

where y1(⋅)y_1(\cdot)y1​(⋅), y0(⋅)y_0(\cdot)y0​(⋅) and x(⋅)x(\cdot)x(⋅) are real-valued (measurable) functions, and WWW can be taken to be one-dimensional without loss of generality. By definition DDD is not an argument of y1y_1y1​, y0y_0y0​ or xxx. Condition 2a is random assignment:

Pr⁡[D=1∣W=w]=p0for all w in the support of W(3)\Pr[D=1|W=w]=p_0\quad\text{for all }w\text{ in the support of }W \tag{3}Pr[D=1∣W=w]=p0​for all w in the support of W(3)

Proposition 1 states that if Conditions 1a and 2a hold, three properties follow. Part (a) is that the distribution of types does not depend on treatment status:

Pr⁡[W≤w∣D=1]=Pr⁡[W≤w∣D=0]=Pr⁡[W≤w],∀w(4)\Pr[W\leq w|D=1]=\Pr[W\leq w|D=0]=\Pr[W\leq w],\quad\forall w \tag{4}Pr[W≤w∣D=1]=Pr[W≤w∣D=0]=Pr[W≤w],∀w(4)

Part (b) is that the difference in means identifies the average treatment effect:

E[Y∣D=1]−E[Y∣D=0]=E[Y1−Y0]=ATE(5)E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=ATE \tag{5}E[Y∣D=1]−E[Y∣D=0]=E[Y1​−Y0​]=ATE(5)

Part (c) is that any pre-determined variable has the same distribution in the two groups:

Pr⁡[X≤x0∣D=1]=Pr⁡[X≤x0∣D=0],∀x0(6)\Pr[X\leq x_0|D=1]=\Pr[X\leq x_0|D=0],\quad\forall x_0 \tag{6}Pr[X≤x0​∣D=1]=Pr[X≤x0​∣D=0],∀x0​(6)

Part (a) is Bayes' rule: because the probability of treatment is the same p0p_0p0​ for every www, conditioning on DDD does not change the distribution of WWW. The paper attributes this step to Condition 1a, but the condition that does the work is Condition 2a. Parts (b) and (c) follow because Y1Y_1Y1​, Y0Y_0Y0​ and XXX are functions of WWW. Part (c) is why analyses of experiments begin by comparing baseline characteristics: Condition 2a generates many testable restrictions.

Assignment by a Score with Imprecise Control

In the RDD the data generating process is different. An individual is drawn after having made his or her optimizing decisions, a score VVV is drawn from a non-degenerate and sufficiently smooth individual-specific distribution, and treatment follows the rule (the threshold is normalized to zero):

D=1[V≥0](7)D=1[V\geq0] \tag{7}D=1[V≥0](7)

Condition 1b keeps the structure of Condition 1a for the pair (W,V)(W,V)(W,V), with WWW unobservable and VVV observable, Y1≡y1(W)Y_1\equiv y_1(W)Y1​≡y1​(W), Y0≡y0(W)Y_0\equiv y_0(W)Y0​≡y0​(W), X≡x(W)X\equiv x(W)X≡x(W), and G(⋅)G(\cdot)G(⋅) the marginal cdf of WWW. Condition 2b is the key assumption. Let F(v∣w)F(v|w)F(v∣w) be the cdf of VVV conditional on WWW. It satisfies:

0<F(0∣w)<1(8)0<F(0|w)<1 \tag{8}0<F(0∣w)<1(8)

and is continuously differentiable in vvv at v=0v=0v=0 for each www in the support of WWW. Let f(⋅)f(\cdot)f(⋅) be the marginal density of VVV and f(⋅∣⋅)f(\cdot|\cdot)f(⋅∣⋅) the density of VVV conditional on WWW, with f(0)>0f(0)>0f(0)>0. Because F(v∣w)F(v|w)F(v∣w) may depend on www in any way, individuals can take actions that change their probability of treatment, and VVV may be arbitrarily correlated with Y1Y_1Y1​, Y0Y_0Y0​ or XXX in the population. The first part of the condition says that nobody is certain to be treated or untreated. The second part says that for each individual the density of the score is continuous at the threshold, so that he or she is as likely to land just below it as just above it.

Part (c) gives the test of the design: if the mean, or any other feature of the distribution, of a pre-determined XXX conditional on VVV changes discontinuously at zero, Condition 1b or Condition 2b must fail.

Allowing the Score to Affect the Outcome

Conditions 1b and 2b have two shortcomings. First, the draw of VVV is not allowed to affect the outcome of a given individual except through treatment, although a test score may affect later outcomes independently of a scholarship. Second, the counterfactuals may not be defined: Y1Y_1Y1​ has no meaning for those with V<0V<0V<0 and Y0Y_0Y0​ none for those with V≥0V\geq0V≥0, just as it makes little sense to speak of the outcome of a Democrat who lost the election with 90 percent of the vote. Condition 1c therefore replaces the two potential outcomes with a response function of the type and the score:

Y≡y(W,V),X≡x(W)(15)Y\equiv y(W,V),\qquad X\equiv x(W) \tag{15}Y≡y(W,V),X≡x(W)(15)

where for each www the function y(⋅,⋅)y(\cdot,\cdot)y(⋅,⋅) is continuous in its second argument except at V=0V=0V=0, where it is only continuous from the right. The individual-specific limits on the two sides of the threshold are:

y−(w)=lim⁡ε→0−y(w,ε),y+(w)=y(w,0)(16)y^-(w)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^-}y(w,\varepsilon),\qquad y^+(w)=y(w,0) \tag{16}y−(w)=ε→0−lim​y(w,ε),y+(w)=y(w,0)(16)

E[Y∣V=0]=∫−∞∞y(w,0)g(w∣0)dw=∫−∞∞y+(w)f(0∣w)f(0)g(w)dw(18)E[Y|V=0]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y(w,0)g(w|0)dw=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y^+(w)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}g(w)dw \tag{18}E[Y∣V=0]=∫−∞∞​y(w,0)g(w∣0)dw=∫−∞∞​y+(w)f(0)f(0∣w)​g(w)dw(18)

and the limit from the left is the same expression with y−(w)y^-(w)y−(w) in place of y+(w)y^+(w)y+(w), because both the response function and the density of types are continuous from the left. In the footnote that gives this argument the paper prints the weight as the product f(0∣w)f(0)f(0|w)f(0)f(0∣w)f(0); the correct weight is the ratio f(0∣w)/f(0)f(0|w)/f(0)f(0∣w)/f(0), as in the proposition itself.

Self-Selection, Random Chance and Complete Control

Condition 2b is linked to the ability of agents to manipulate VVV around the threshold. If, for a non-trivial fraction of the population, the density of VVV is discontinuous at the cutoff, parts (a), (b) and (c) of Propositions 2 and 3 generally fail. Suppose that some students taking a scholarship examination know with certainty whether each answer is correct, care only about winning, and find time in the examination costly. They answer exactly the minimum number of questions (say 70) correctly, the density of their score is discontinuous at the cutoff, and the RDD is inappropriate. If instead the questions that appear, or how sharp the student feels that day, are beyond the student's control, Condition 2b is plausible. The difference is formalized by writing the score as the sum of two components:

V=Z+e(19)V=Z+e \tag{19}V=Z+e(19)

where ZZZ is the systematic or predictable component, which can depend on the individual's attributes and actions (such as effort in studying), and eee is an exogenous random chance component with a continuous density. Under complete control there is no eee; with any eee, however small, chance influences the final score. Local random assignment therefore survives endogenous sorting as long as agents cannot sort precisely around the threshold. If they can, the density of VVV is likely to be discontinuous, especially when treatment is beneficial. The conclusion adds that the marginal density of VVV itself can be examined for a discontinuity (McCrary 2004).

Relation to Selection Models

The mechanism is implicitly present in standard econometric evaluation models, except that there the score is not observed. In the reduced form of the dummy endogenous-variable model of Heckman (1978):

y1=x1α1+dβ+u1y2∗=x2α2+u2d=1[y2∗≥0](20)\begin{aligned} y_1&=x_1\alpha_1+d\beta+u_1\\ y_2^*&=x_2\alpha_2+u_2\\ d&=1[y_2^*\geq0] \end{aligned} \tag{20}y1​y2∗​d​=x1​α1​+dβ+u1​=x2​α2​+u2​=1[y2∗​≥0]​(20)

y1y_1y1​ is the outcome, ddd the treatment indicator, x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​ exogenous variables, and (u1,u2)(u_1,u_2)(u1​,u2​) errors that are typically assumed bivariate normal and jointly independent of x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​, with an exclusion restriction that x2x_2x2​ contains variables absent from x1x_1x1​. The model satisfies Conditions 1b and 2b with:

V=y2∗,Y1=x1α1+β+u1,Y0=x1α1+u1,D=d(21)V=y_2^*,\qquad Y_1=x_1\alpha_1+\beta+u_1,\qquad Y_0=x_1\alpha_1+u_1,\qquad D=d \tag{21}V=y2∗​,Y1​=x1​α1​+β+u1​,Y0​=x1​α1​+u1​,D=d(21)

(the paper writes the error in Y1Y_1Y1​ and Y0Y_0Y0​ as uuu without a subscript). When y2∗y_2^*y2∗​ is unobservable, everything depends on correct specification: the choice of x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​, the independence assumption and the exclusion restriction. Any mis-specification biases the estimates of α1\alpha_1α1​, α2\alpha_2α2​ and β\betaβ. When the researcher observes y2∗y_2^*y2∗​, as in the RDD, none of the variables in x1x_1x1​ or x2x_2x2​ is needed to estimate β\betaβ and the errors need not be independent of anything. The covariates take on two different roles. They test Condition 2b through the gap:

E[x1∣y2∗=0]−lim⁡Δ→0−E[x1∣y2∗=Δ](22)E[x_1|y_2^*=0]-\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E[x_1|y_2^*=\Delta] \tag{22}E[x1​∣y2∗​=0]−Δ→0−lim​E[x1​∣y2∗​=Δ](22)

which should be zero under local random assignment, and they can be added to the regression to reduce sampling variability without changing what is estimated, as baseline covariates are in an experiment. This is the contrast with strategies that rely on conditioning on observables or on a correctly specified selection equation: there the covariates are needed for identification, here they are over-identifying checks. The argument does not depend on linear indices, joint normality or a constant treatment effect.

Incumbency Advantage: Estimand and Model

The incumbency advantage is defined as the overall causal impact of being the current incumbent party in a district on the votes obtained in the district's election; the unit of observation is the congressional district. The raw facts are striking. The incumbent party wins about 90 percent of the time, with a two-party vote share of about 60 to 70 percent. A winning candidate has about an 80 percent chance of both running again and winning (about 88 percent run, and about 90 percent of those win), against about 3 percent for the runner-up, who runs again with probability of about 20 percent. These differences need not be causal: as Erikson (1971) noted, incumbents are by definition the politicians who succeeded in the previous election, and whatever made them succeed persists. The model of two consecutive elections is:

vi2=αwi1+βvi1+γdi2+ei2di2=1[vi1≥12]E[ei2∣wi1,vi1]=0(23)\begin{aligned} v_{i2}&=\alpha w_{i1}+\beta v_{i1}+\gamma d_{i2}+e_{i2}\\ d_{i2}&=1\left[v_{i1}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\right]\\ E[e_{i2}|w_{i1},v_{i1}]&=0 \end{aligned} \tag{23}vi2​di2​E[ei2​∣wi1​,vi1​]​=αwi1​+βvi1​+γdi2​+ei2​=1[vi1​≥21​]=0​(23)

together with the assumption that fi1(v∣w)f_{i1}(v|w)fi1​(v∣w), the density of vi1v_{i1}vi1​ conditional on wi1w_{i1}wi1​, is continuous in vvv. Here vitv_{it}vit​ is the Democratic vote share in district iii in election year ttt, di2d_{i2}di2​ indicates that the Democrats are the incumbent party during the race in year 2, and wi1w_{i1}wi1​ is a vector of all characteristics determined, and all choices made by agents, as of election day in year 1 (partisan make-up of the district, party resources, quality of potential nominees). The vote share vi1v_{i1}vi1​ may itself affect vi2v_{i2}vi2​, for instance by attracting donors. The parameter of interest is γ\gammaγ, the electoral advantage to incumbency. OLS is biased because elements of wi1w_{i1}wi1​ are unobserved and correlated with vi1v_{i1}vi1​ and hence with di2d_{i2}di2​. The model is a special case of Condition 1c with W=wi1W=w_{i1}W=wi1​, V=vi1V=v_{i1}V=vi1​ and the threshold at one half:

Y=y(W,V)=αW+βV+γ⋅1[V≥12],γ=y(w,12)−lim⁡ε→0+y(w,12−ε)(24)Y=y(W,V)=\alpha W+\beta V+\gamma\cdot1\left[V\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\right],\qquad\gamma=y\left(w,\tfrac{1}{2}\right)-\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}y\left(w,\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon\right) \tag{24}Y=y(W,V)=αW+βV+γ⋅1[V≥21​],γ=y(w,21​)−ε→0+lim​y(w,21​−ε)(24)

The observed outcome is vi2=Y+ei2v_{i2}=Y+e_{i2}vi2​=Y+ei2​, and since the error has mean zero conditional on VVV and WWW:

E[vi2∣vi1]=E[Y∣vi1](25)E[v_{i2}|v_{i1}]=E[Y|v_{i1}] \tag{25}E[vi2​∣vi1​]=E[Y∣vi1​](25)

so Proposition 3 applies. The crucial assumption is that, even if agents influence the vote, the final vote share has a random chance component with a continuous density conditional on their choices and characteristics; weather on election day that affects turnout is an example. This requires that certain kinds of electoral fraud are negligible. If a non-trivial fraction of Democrats (and no Republicans) could perfectly predict the true count and selectively invalidate opponents' ballots only when the true count would produce a Republican win, the density of vi1v_{i1}vi1​ would be discontinuous at one half. Fraud that stops when 90 percent of the vote is counted would leave the density continuous, because the remaining tally is still unpredictable. Proposition 3(c) makes the question empirical: under the first kind of fraud, characteristics determined before year 1 would differ across the threshold.

Data and Estimation

The data are candidate-level returns for U.S. House elections from 1946 to 1998 (ICPSR study 7757, extended with returns from the Office of the Clerk for 1992 to 1998). The outcome vi2v_{i2}vi2​ is dated from 1948 to 1998 and the score vi1v_{i1}vi1​ from 1946 to 1996. Because of decennial redistricting, and because both leads and lags of the vote share are used, years ending in 0 and 2 are dropped as score years. The district-level data set has 6558 observations (3818 Democratic wins and 2740 losses), of which 610 are decided by a margin of less than 5 percent of the vote (322 wins and 288 losses); the candidate-level data set, which can use more years, has 9674 Democratic observations. Because third parties obtain some votes, the score is the Democratic vote share margin of victory, the Democratic share minus the share of the strongest opponent, with threshold zero. Uncontested candidates are assigned a share of one and the opposing party zero; in about 3 percent of possible elections no candidate is reported, and the outcome is imputed by the state-year or state-decade average. Candidates are matched over time by a name algorithm; in a hand-checked sample 0.982 of true observations are matched and 0.992 of matches are true. Standard errors are clustered at the decade-district level. Results are reported for Democrats only, since in a two-party system the Republican results are the mirror image.

Four outcomes in election t+1t+1t+1 are studied: the probability that the candidate both becomes the nominee and wins, the probability that the candidate becomes the nominee, the party's vote share irrespective of nominee, and the probability that the party wins the seat. The first two measure the effect on the candidate's political future and the last two the effect on the party's hold on the seat. The analysis is at the party-district level because candidates are not compelled to run again, and this selective drop-out would corrupt even a truly randomized experiment for candidate-level vote outcomes. The figures plot local averages in bins of width 0.005 of the margin together with a parametric fit. The paper writes no estimating equation: the discontinuity gap is estimated by regressing the outcome on a fourth-order polynomial in the margin of victory separately on each side of the threshold, equivalently on the victory indicator, the quartic and their interactions, and the figures use a logit fit for binary outcomes. The parametric fit is needed because the difference in means within a narrow window is a biased estimate of the gap when the conditional expectation has a non-zero slope; local linear regression (Hahn, Todd and van der Klaauw 2001) and the estimator of Porter (2003) are mentioned as alternatives.

Main Estimates and Balance

  • Candidate outcomes: the probability that a Democrat both runs in and wins election t+1t+1t+1 jumps by about 0.45 at the threshold, and the probability of remaining the party's nominee by about 0.40 (the introduction gives 0.43 as the deterrence effect of losing). No jump is visible anywhere else.

  • Party outcomes: the parametric fit gives a Democratic vote share in t+1t+1t+1 of 0.531 just above and 0.454 just below the threshold, a gap of 0.077 (standard error 0.011). The probability that the party wins the seat is 0.611 just above and 0.253 just below, a gap of about 0.36; the text describes this effect as about 0.35 when reading the figure and as about 0.38 across the regression specifications, and the introduction summarizes the probability effects as 0.40 to 0.45.

  • Selection in the raw comparison: across all elections, Democratic winners obtain a vote share of 0.698 in t+1t+1t+1 against 0.347 for losers, and win with probability 0.909 against 0.094. They also differ before the election: the vote share in t−1t-1t−1 is 0.681 against 0.368, the probability of having won in t−1t-1t−1 is 0.889 against 0.109, and the candidate's number of past victories is 3.812 against 0.261. All outcomes rise with the margin on both sides of the threshold, which is the selection bias of a simple comparison of means.

  • Balance: the pre-determined differences shrink as elections get closer but do not vanish within a 5 percent margin (vote share in t−1t-1t−1 of 0.501 against 0.474, win probability in t−1t-1t−1 of 0.501 against 0.365, past victories of 1.658 against 0.986). With the polynomial fit they disappear: 0.477 against 0.481 for the lagged vote share, 0.419 against 0.416 for the lagged win probability, 1.219 against 1.183 for the Democrat's past victories, 1.424 against 1.293 for the opponent's, 1.485 against 1.470 for the Democrat's past election attempts and 1.624 against 1.502 for the opponent's. None of these differences is statistically significant.

  • Covariates: the vote-share estimate is 0.077 with no controls, 0.078 with the lagged vote share and lagged win indicator (the lagged share has a coefficient of 0.293 with standard error 0.017), 0.077 with either set of experience variables and 0.078 with all controls. It is 0.081 (0.014) when the outcome is the residual from a regression of the vote share on all pre-determined variables, and 0.079 (0.013) when the outcome is the change in vote share between t−1t-1t−1 and t+1t+1t+1.

  • Refutability test: the estimated effect of winning in ttt on the vote share in t−1t-1t−1 is −0.002-0.002−0.002 (0.011), and on the probability of a Democratic win in t−1t-1t−1 it is −0.005-0.005−0.005 (0.033).

The mild continuity assumption thus delivers local independence, which has in principle infinitely many testable implications (one for each pre-determined variable and each moment), and the election data pass those examined. The causal estimates depend on this quasi-random assignment: the gaps in t+1t+1t+1 outcomes are interpreted as effects only because the same procedure finds no gaps in anything determined before election ttt.

Comparison with Existing Incumbency Measures

The RDD identifies an incumbent party advantage: the electoral gain to the party from being the incumbent party in a district, relative to not being it. The political science literature mostly measures an incumbent legislator advantage: the gain to the party from having the incumbent legislator run again, relative to a new candidate of the same party in the same district (Gelman and King 1990). The party advantage includes the legislator advantage as one mechanism, because a narrow win raises the probability that the nominee runs as an incumbent in the next election, and it also includes the gain that arises because the party holds the seat. Appendix B compares the approaches in a diagram of the average Democratic vote share in period 2, V2V_2V2​, against the share in period 1, V1V_1V1​. The sophomore surge takes first-time Democratic incumbents and subtracts their average period-1 share from their average period-2 share:

Soph.Surge=V2‾−V1‾(26)\text{Soph.Surge}=\overline{V_2}-\overline{V_1} \tag{26}Soph.Surge=V2​​−V1​​(26)

The retirement slump takes districts whose seat is open in period 2 and subtracts the average share of the incoming candidate from the average share of the retiring incumbent:

R.Slump=V1‾−V2‾(27)\text{R.Slump}=\overline{V_1}-\overline{V_2} \tag{27}R.Slump=V1​​−V2​​(27)

where the averages are now taken over the districts with open seats. The Gelman-King index, which the appendix labels ψ\psiψ, is the vertical gap between the line for districts in which the incumbent seeks re-election and the parallel line for open seats, controlling for V1V_1V1​. The RD estimate, which the appendix labels β\betaβ although the model above calls the same parameter γ\gammaγ, is the jump in the line for all seats at 0.50. It answers how the party would have performed in period 2 had it lost in period 1, using the districts that barely missed being incumbent. There is no necessary connection between the measures: the RD gap could be zero while the other three are significant, or large while they are zero. The three legislator measures also require defeats or open seats, so in a year in which every incumbent ran again only the RD measure could be estimated. In an earlier draft a bounding analysis suggested that most of the incumbency advantage may reflect a quality-of-candidate selection effect, through the effect of losing on drop-out.

This is the observation rule of the potential-outcomes framework. Each individual carries two outcomes: Y1Y_1Y1​, what would happen with treatment, and Y0Y_0Y0​, what would happen without it. The indicator DDD equals one for a treated individual and zero otherwise, so the formula simply selects the relevant potential outcome:

Y={Y1if D=1Y0if D=0Y=\begin{cases}Y_1 & \text{if } D=1\\ Y_0 & \text{if } D=0\end{cases}Y={Y1​Y0​​if D=1if D=0​

The individual causal effect is Y1−Y0Y_1-Y_0Y1​−Y0​, but only one of the two terms is ever observed for a given individual, which is the fundamental problem of causal inference. The equation rules out interference between individuals and multiple versions of treatment: the outcome depends on the individual's own DDD only. It also implies E[Y∣D=1]=E[Y1∣D=1]E[Y|D=1]=E[Y_1|D=1]E[Y∣D=1]=E[Y1​∣D=1] and E[Y∣D=0]=E[Y0∣D=0]E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_0|D=0]E[Y∣D=0]=E[Y0​∣D=0], the two facts used to derive equation (5). The same rule is used in the regression-discontinuity setting once DDD is generated by equation (7); there it is the reason why E[Y∣V=v]E[Y|V=v]E[Y∣V=v] equals an average of y1y_1y1​ for v≥0v\geq0v≥0 and of y0y_0y0​ for v<0v<0v<0, as in equations (13) and (14). Equation (15) later replaces the pair (Y1,Y0)(Y_1,Y_0)(Y1​,Y0​) by a response function of the score because the two potential outcomes may not be well defined far from the threshold.

This is Condition 1a of the paper. It introduces an unobservable random variable WWW, the type or identity of the individual drawn from the population, and makes the potential outcomes and the baseline variable deterministic functions of it: y1(⋅)y_1(\cdot)y1​(⋅), y0(⋅)y_0(\cdot)y0​(⋅) and x(⋅)x(\cdot)x(⋅) are fixed measurable real-valued functions, and all randomness in (Y1,Y0,X)(Y_1,Y_0,X)(Y1​,Y0​,X) comes from the draw of WWW. Nothing is lost by this: one may always take WWW to be the individual's label, or the vector (Y1,Y0,X)(Y_1,Y_0,X)(Y1​,Y0​,X) itself, and the paper notes that WWW can be taken one-dimensional without loss of generality.

What the condition buys is a clean separation of two sources of randomness: who is drawn (the distribution GGG of WWW) and how treatment is assigned given who was drawn (the conditional distribution of DDD, or later of VVV, given WWW). What it rules out is that DDD enters the functions: DDD is not an argument of y1y_1y1​ or y0y_0y0​ by the definition of potential outcomes, and it is not an argument of xxx because XXX is determined before assignment. Consequently any statement about the distribution of WWW transfers at once to Y1Y_1Y1​, Y0Y_0Y0​ and XXX; this is how equations (5) and (6) follow from equation (4), and how equations (10) and (11) follow from equation (9). For example,

This is Condition 2a, random assignment. The left-hand side is the propensity to be treated for an individual of type www; the condition says that it is the same number p0p_0p0​ for every type. It is a statement about the assignment mechanism (a lottery with known odds), not about outcomes, which is why its plausibility is easy to judge in a real experiment. For the conditional probabilities in equation (4) to be defined one needs 0<p0<10<p_0<10<p0​<1, which the paper leaves implicit.

This is the treatment rule of a sharp regression-discontinuity design. VVV is the observed score (running variable) and 1[⋅]1[\cdot]1[⋅] is the indicator function, so D=1D=1D=1 exactly when the score is at or above the threshold. The threshold v0v_0v0​ of the introduction is normalized to zero, which is without loss of generality because one can always redefine the score as V−v0V-v_0V−v0​; in the election application the score is the Democratic margin of victory, whose threshold is naturally zero, and in equation (23) the same rule appears with the vote share and the threshold one half.

Two features matter. First, DDD is a deterministic function of VVV: conditional on the score there is no randomness left in treatment, so there is no overlap between treated and untreated at any value of VVV, and matching on VVV is impossible. All identification must come from comparing values of VVV on the two sides of zero. Second, the inequality is weak, so individuals with V=0V=0V=0 are treated; this is why the paper evaluates the treated side at V=0V=0V=0 exactly and the untreated side as a limit from the left, lim⁡Δ→0−E[Y∣V=Δ]\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E[Y|V=\Delta]limΔ→0−​E[Y∣V=Δ], in equations (10) and (17). Combined with equation (1), the rule gives Y=y1(W)Y=y_1(W)Y=y1​(W) for V≥0V\geq0V≥0 and Y=y0(W)Y=y_0(W)Y=y0​(W) for V<0V<0V<0. The treatment probability of type www is Pr⁡[V≥0∣W=w]=1−F(0∣w)\Pr[V\geq0|W=w]=1-F(0|w)Pr[V≥0∣W=w]=1−F(0∣w), which is where equation (8) enters.

This is the first half of Condition 2b. F(v∣w)=Pr⁡[V≤v∣W=w]F(v|w)=\Pr[V\leq v|W=w]F(v∣w)=Pr[V≤v∣W=w] is the cdf of the score for an individual of type www, so F(0∣w)F(0|w)F(0∣w) is that individual's probability of ending up at or below the threshold; since the conditional distribution is continuous at zero, it is the probability of not being treated. The inequality says that every type has a probability of treatment strictly between zero and one: the score is a non-degenerate random variable for everyone, and no one is certain to be treated or untreated. The probability 1−F(0∣w)1-F(0|w)1−F(0∣w) may differ arbitrarily across types, which is how the condition allows self-selection.

The second half of Condition 2b, stated in the text, is that F(v∣w)F(v|w)F(v∣w) is continuously differentiable in vvv at v=0v=0v=0 for each www, that is, the individual density f(v∣w)f(v|w)f(v∣w) is continuous at the threshold. This is the assumption of imprecise control, and it is what delivers local randomization. For a type with f(0∣w)>0f(0|w)>0f(0∣w)>0 and a small window h>0h>0h>0,

Pr⁡[V≥0 ∣ −h<V<h, W=w]=∫0hf(v∣w) dv∫−hhf(v∣w) dv ⟶ f(0∣w)2f(0∣w)=12as h→0\Pr[V\geq0\,|\,-h<V<h,\ W=w]=\frac{\int_{0}^{h}f(v|w)\,dv}{\int_{-h}^{h}f(v|w)\,dv}\ \longrightarrow\ \frac{f(0|w)}{2f(0|w)}=\frac{1}{2}\quad\text{as }h\to0Pr[V≥0∣−h<V<h, W=w]=∫−hh​f(v∣w)dv∫0h​f(v∣w)dv​ ⟶ 2f(0∣w)f(0∣w)​=21​as h→0

so, conditional on being close to the threshold, every such type is treated with the same probability one half. The paper states Proposition 2(a) as: Pr⁡[W≤w∣V=v]\Pr[W\leq w|V=v]Pr[W≤w∣V=v] is continuous in vvv at v=0v=0v=0 for all www. A function is continuous at a point exactly when its left limit and its right limit exist and both equal its value there, so equation (9) is an equivalent restatement. To prove it, take WWW continuous with density ggg and use the conditional density from equation (12):

lim⁡v→0f(v∣z) g(z)=f(0∣z) g(z)for each z\lim_{v\to0}f(v|z)\,g(z)=f(0|z)\,g(z)\quad\text{for each }zv→0lim​f(v∣z)g(z)=f(0∣z)g(z)for each z

Remark on an unstated regularity condition. Pointwise continuity of f(v∣z)f(v|z)f(v∣z) for each zzz does not by itself allow the limit to be taken inside the integral over zzz; one needs, for example, a function m(z)m(z)m(z) with f(v∣z)≤m(z)f(v|z)\leq m(z)f(v∣z)≤m(z) for all vvv near zero and ∫m(z)g(z) dz<∞\int m(z)g(z)\,dz<\infty∫m(z)g(z)dz<∞ (dominated convergence). The paper's footnote and the note both treat continuity of f(v)f(v)f(v) as immediate from Condition 2b.

The first equality. At V=0V=0V=0 everyone is treated, and by equation (13) the mean outcome there is E[Y1∣V=0]E[Y_1|V=0]E[Y1​∣V=0]. Hence

E[Y∣V=0]−lim⁡Δ→0−E[Y∣V=Δ]=E[Y1∣V=0]−E[Y0∣V=0]=E[Y1−Y0∣V=0]E[Y|V=0]-\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E[Y|V=\Delta]=E[Y_1|V=0]-E[Y_0|V=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0|V=0]E[Y∣V=0]−Δ→0−lim​E[Y∣V=Δ]=E[Y1​∣V=0]−E[Y0​∣V=0]=E[Y1​−Y0​∣V=0]

The second equality. Subtract equation (14) from equation (13) and collect terms under one integral:

E[Y1−Y0∣V=0]=∫−∞∞y1(w)f(0∣w)f(0)g(w) dw−∫−∞∞y0(w)f(0∣w)f(0)g(w) dw=∫−∞∞(y1(w)−y0(w))f(0∣w)f(0) g(w) dw=∫−∞∞(y1(w)−y0(w))f(0∣w)f(0) dG(w)\begin{aligned} E[Y_1-Y_0|V=0]&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y_1(w)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}g(w)\,dw-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y_0(w)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}g(w)\,dw\\ &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(y_1(w)-y_0(w)\right)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}\,g(w)\,dw\\ &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(y_1(w)-y_0(w)\right)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}\,dG(w) \end{aligned}E[Y1​−Y0​∣V=0]​=∫−∞∞​y1​(w)f(0)f(0∣w)​g(w)dw−∫−∞∞​y0​(w)f(0)f(0∣w)​g(w)dw=∫−∞∞​(y1​(w)−y0​(w))f(0)f(0∣w)​g(w)dw=∫−∞∞​(y1​(w)−y0​(w))f(0)f(0∣w)​dG(w)​

using dG(w)=g(w) dwdG(w)=g(w)\,dwdG(w)=g(w)dw. This defines ATE∗ATE^*ATE∗. ∫−∞∞f(0∣w)f(0) dG(w)=1f(0)∫−∞∞f(0∣w) dG(w)=f(0)f(0)=1\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}\,dG(w)=\frac{1}{f(0)}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(0|w)\,dG(w)=\frac{f(0)}{f(0)}=1∫−∞∞​f(0)f(0∣w)​dG(w)=f(0)1​∫−∞∞​f(0∣w)dG(w)=f(0)f(0)​=1

so ATE∗ATE^*ATE∗ is a genuine weighted average of the individual effects y1(w)−y0(w)y_1(w)-y_0(w)y1​(w)−y0​(w). The paper states Proposition 2(c) as: Pr⁡[X≤x0∣V=v]\Pr[X\leq x_0|V=v]Pr[X≤x0​∣V=v] is continuous in vvv at v=0v=0v=0 for all x0x_0x0​. Pr⁡[X≤x0∣V=v]=Pr⁡[x(W)≤x0∣V=v]=∫−∞∞1[x(w)≤x0] g(w∣v) dw\Pr[X\leq x_0|V=v]=\Pr[x(W)\leq x_0|V=v]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}1[x(w)\leq x_0]\,g(w|v)\,dwPr[X≤x0​∣V=v]=Pr[x(W)≤x0​∣V=v]=∫−∞∞​1[x(w)≤x0​]g(w∣v)dw

lim⁡v↑0Pr⁡[X≤x0∣V=v]=∫−∞∞1[x(w)≤x0] g(w∣0) dw=lim⁡v↓0Pr⁡[X≤x0∣V=v]\lim_{v\uparrow0}\Pr[X\leq x_0|V=v]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}1[x(w)\leq x_0]\,g(w|0)\,dw=\lim_{v\downarrow0}\Pr[X\leq x_0|V=v]v↑0lim​Pr[X≤x0​∣V=v]=∫−∞∞​1[x(w)≤x0​]g(w∣0)dw=v↓0lim​Pr[X≤x0​∣V=v]

The logic is the same as for equation (6): the distribution of types is the same just below and just above the threshold, and XXX is a function of the type. The result therefore rests on part (a), equation (9), or more precisely on the continuity of g(w∣v)g(w|v)g(w∣v) that proves it. The paper's text says that (c) follows from (b); that cannot be right, since (b), equation (10), concerns the mean of YYY and says nothing about XXX. The note's remark is correct. The testable implication is that the mean of any pre-determined variable satisfies E[X∣V=0]−lim⁡Δ→0−E[X∣V=Δ]=0E[X|V=0]-\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E[X|V=\Delta]=0E[X∣V=0]−limΔ→0−​E[X∣V=Δ]=0, which is used in equation (22) and in the balance tables.

Let h(w,v)h(w,v)h(w,v) denote the joint density of the type and the score. It can be factored in two ways, conditioning on either variable:

h(w,v)=f(v∣w) g(w)=g(w∣v) f(v)h(w,v)=f(v|w)\,g(w)=g(w|v)\,f(v)h(w,v)=f(v∣w)g(w)=g(w∣v)f(v)

The first factorization follows the data generating process (draw a type from ggg, then draw a score from that type's density); the second conditions on the observed score. Solving for the density of types among individuals with score vvv, for any vvv with f(v)>0f(v)>0f(v)>0:

g(w∣v)=f(v∣w) g(w)f(v)g(w|v)=\frac{f(v|w)\,g(w)}{f(v)}g(w∣v)=f(v)f(v∣w)g(w)​

which is equation (12), Bayes' rule for densities. The denominator is the marginal density of the score, obtained by integrating the joint density over types:

f(v)=∫−∞∞h(w,v) dw=∫−∞∞f(v∣w) g(w) dwf(v)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(w,v)\,dw=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(v|w)\,g(w)\,dwf(v)=∫−∞∞​h(w,v)dw=∫−∞∞​f(v∣w)g(w)dw

so g(w∣v)g(w|v)g(w∣v) integrates to one over www. The formula says that the population observed at score vvv is the original population reweighted by f(v∣w)/f(v)f(v|w)/f(v)f(v∣w)/f(v): types that are likely to draw the score vvv are over-represented there. Since the reweighting factor depends on www in general, the population at a given score is selected. What Condition 2b adds is that the reweighting factor changes continuously as vvv crosses zero, so the selected population just below the threshold is the same as the one just above.

At V=0V=0V=0 the rule in equation (7) gives D=1D=1D=1, so by equation (1) the observed outcome is Y=Y1Y=Y_1Y=Y1​, and by Condition 1b, Y1=y1(W)Y_1=y_1(W)Y1​=y1​(W):

E[Y∣V=0]=E[Y1∣V=0]=E[y1(W)∣V=0]E[Y|V=0]=E[Y_1|V=0]=E[y_1(W)|V=0]E[Y∣V=0]=E[Y1​∣V=0]=E[y1​(W)∣V=0]

which is equation (13). No limit is needed on this side because the threshold itself belongs to the treated region. The expression is the mean treated outcome in the population reweighted by f(0∣w)/f(0)f(0|w)/f(0)f(0∣w)/f(0); it differs from the population mean E[Y1]E[Y_1]E[Y1​] whenever types with different y1(w)y_1(w)y1​(w) have different densities at the threshold.

Taking the limit inside the integral gives

which is equation (14). The right-hand side is a counterfactual: the mean untreated outcome of the individuals who are at the threshold and therefore treated. It is identified because the untreated individuals just below the threshold have the same distribution of types.

Remark on an unstated regularity condition. The interchange of limit and integral ("by continuity" in the paper) requires more than pointwise convergence of the weight. It is valid if y0y_0y0​ is bounded and f(v)f(v)f(v) is continuous at zero, or more generally if ∣y0(w)∣f(Δ∣w)|y_0(w)|f(\Delta|w)∣y0​(w)∣f(Δ∣w) is dominated, for Δ\DeltaΔ near zero, by a function that is integrable with respect to GGG.

This is Condition 1c, which generalizes Condition 1b. Instead of two potential outcomes that depend only on the type, the outcome is a response function y(w,v)y(w,v)y(w,v) of the type and of the realized score: an individual of type www who draws score vvv has outcome y(w,v)y(w,v)y(w,v). The baseline variable is still a function of the type alone, X=x(W)X=x(W)X=x(W), because it is determined before the score is drawn. The function y(⋅,⋅)y(\cdot,\cdot)y(⋅,⋅) is assumed continuous in its second argument everywhere except at the threshold, where it is only continuous from the right; treatment status is absorbed into the dependence on vvv, and its effect is the possible jump at zero defined in equation (16).

The form answers two objections to equation (2). First, the score may affect the outcome directly: an examination score may matter for later outcomes independently of a scholarship, and a vote share may attract donors. Condition 1b rules this out, Condition 1c allows any continuous direct effect. Second, y1(w)y_1(w)y1​(w) for an individual far below the threshold, or y0(w)y_0(w)y0​(w) for one far above, may have no meaning; y(w,v)y(w,v)y(w,v) never requires such objects. Condition 1b is the special case

y(w,v)=y0(w)+1[v≥0](y1(w)−y0(w))y(w,v)=y_0(w)+1[v\geq0]\left(y_1(w)-y_0(w)\right)y(w,v)=y0​(w)+1[v≥0](y1​(w)−y0​(w))

which is flat in vvv on each side of zero. What the form rules out is a direct effect of the score that is itself discontinuous at zero for reasons other than the treatment; continuity in vvv is what separates the treatment effect from the direct effect. The election model, equations (23) and (24), is an instance with y(w,v)y(w,v)y(w,v) linear in vvv.

These are the two one-sided values of the response function of equation (15) at the threshold, for a given type www. The first, y−(w)y^-(w)y−(w), is the limit of the outcome as the score approaches zero from below: what the individual would obtain with a score infinitesimally short of the threshold, hence untreated. The second, y+(w)y^+(w)y+(w), is the outcome with a score exactly at the threshold, hence treated; since y(w,⋅)y(w,\cdot)y(w,⋅) is continuous from the right at zero, it is also the limit from above:

y+(w)=y(w,0)=lim⁡ε→0+y(w,ε)y^+(w)=y(w,0)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}y(w,\varepsilon)y+(w)=y(w,0)=ε→0+lim​y(w,ε)

The individual-specific discontinuity gap y+(w)−y−(w)y^+(w)-y^-(w)y+(w)−y−(w) is the causal effect of interest for type www: the effect of crossing the threshold holding the individual, and essentially the score, fixed. Any direct effect of the score is continuous and therefore cancels in the difference. Under the special case of Condition 1b the definitions reduce to y+(w)=y1(w)y^+(w)=y_1(w)y+(w)=y1​(w) and y−(w)=y0(w)y^-(w)=y_0(w)y−(w)=y0​(w), and the gap is the usual treatment effect.

A numerical illustration: if y(w,v)=w+0.3v+0.08⋅1[v≥0]y(w,v)=w+0.3v+0.08\cdot1[v\geq0]y(w,v)=w+0.3v+0.08⋅1[v≥0], then y−(w)=wy^-(w)=wy−(w)=w and y+(w)=w+0.08y^+(w)=w+0.08y+(w)=w+0.08, so the gap is 0.08 for every type even though the outcome also rises with the score at rate 0.3. The gaps are averaged in equation (17) with weights f(0∣w)/f(0)f(0|w)/f(0)f(0∣w)/f(0), and y+(w)y^+(w)y+(w) appears in equation (18). In the election model, equation (24), the gap is the constant γ\gammaγ.

The right side of the threshold is equation (18):

E[Y∣V=0]=∫−∞∞y+(w)f(0∣w)f(0)g(w) dwE[Y|V=0]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y^+(w)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}g(w)\,dwE[Y∣V=0]=∫−∞∞​y+(w)f(0)f(0∣w)​g(w)dw

For the left side take Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0. By equation (15), Y=y(W,V)Y=y(W,V)Y=y(W,V), and by Bayes' rule, equation (12):

E[Y∣V=Δ]=∫−∞∞y(w,Δ) g(w∣Δ) dw=∫−∞∞y(w,Δ)f(Δ∣w)f(Δ)g(w) dwE[Y|V=\Delta]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y(w,\Delta)\,g(w|\Delta)\,dw=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y(w,\Delta)\frac{f(\Delta|w)}{f(\Delta)}g(w)\,dwE[Y∣V=Δ]=∫−∞∞​y(w,Δ)g(w∣Δ)dw=∫−∞∞​y(w,Δ)f(Δ)f(Δ∣w)​g(w)dw

Let Δ→0−\Delta\to0^-Δ→0−. Now two pieces of the integrand move: y(w,Δ)→y−(w)y(w,\Delta)\to y^-(w)y(w,Δ)→y−(w) by the definition in equation (16), and f(Δ∣w)/f(Δ)→f(0∣w)/f(0)f(\Delta|w)/f(\Delta)\to f(0|w)/f(0)f(Δ∣w)/f(Δ)→f(0∣w)/f(0) by Condition 2b. Taking the limit inside the integral (under the same domination condition as for equation (14)):

lim⁡Δ→0−E[Y∣V=Δ]=∫−∞∞y−(w)f(0∣w)f(0)g(w) dw\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E[Y|V=\Delta]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y^-(w)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}g(w)\,dwΔ→0−lim​E[Y∣V=Δ]=∫−∞∞​y−(w)f(0)f(0∣w)​g(w)dw

E[Y∣V=0]−lim⁡Δ→0−E[Y∣V=Δ]=∫−∞∞(y+(w)−y−(w))f(0∣w)f(0) dG(w)=ATE∗∗E[Y|V=0]-\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E[Y|V=\Delta]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(y^+(w)-y^-(w)\right)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}\,dG(w)=ATE^{**}E[Y∣V=0]−Δ→0−lim​E[Y∣V=Δ]=∫−∞∞​(y+(w)−y−(w))f(0)f(0∣w)​dG(w)=ATE∗∗

which is equation (17). The weights are the same as in equation (10) and integrate to one. With y+=y1y^+=y_1y+=y1​ and y−=y0y^-=y_0y−=y0​ the formula reduces to equation (10).

On the paper's footnote 10. The footnote prints the weight as the product f(0∣w)f(0)f(0|w)f(0)f(0∣w)f(0). Under Condition 1c, equation (15), the outcome of an individual of type www whose score is exactly zero is y(w,0)y(w,0)y(w,0). Conditioning on V=0V=0V=0 and integrating over the distribution of types at the threshold:

E[Y∣V=0]=E[y(W,V)∣V=0]=E[y(W,0)∣V=0]=∫−∞∞y(w,0) g(w∣0) dwE[Y|V=0]=E[y(W,V)|V=0]=E[y(W,0)|V=0]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y(w,0)\,g(w|0)\,dwE[Y∣V=0]=E[y(W,V)∣V=0]=E[y(W,0)∣V=0]=∫−∞∞​y(w,0)g(w∣0)dw

g(w∣0)=f(0∣w) g(w)f(0)g(w|0)=\frac{f(0|w)\,g(w)}{f(0)}g(w∣0)=f(0)f(0∣w)g(w)​

The paper's footnote 10 prints the product f(0∣w)f(0)f(0|w)f(0)f(0∣w)f(0) in this expression and in the companion expression for the left limit; with the product the right-hand side would equal f(0)2E[Y∣V=0]f(0)^2E[Y|V=0]f(0)2E[Y∣V=0], so the printed version is a typographical error and the note's ratio is correct.

This decomposition formalizes the difference between imprecise and complete control of the score. ZZZ is the systematic or predictable component: everything about the score that the individual determines or can foresee, such as ability and effort in preparing for an examination, or a party's resources and candidate quality. It may depend on the type in any way and may be chosen strategically. The term eee is an exogenous random chance component that the individual cannot predict or control (which questions appear, the weather on election day), assumed to have a continuous density.

The link to Condition 2b is direct. Take ZZZ to be a function Z(w)Z(w)Z(w) of the type and let eee have density fe(⋅∣w)f_e(\cdot|w)fe​(⋅∣w) given the type. Then the type-specific density of the score is a shifted copy of the density of the chance component:

f(v∣w)=fe(v−Z(w) ∣ w)f(v|w)=f_e\left(v-Z(w)\,|\,w\right)f(v∣w)=fe​(v−Z(w)∣w)

which is continuous in vvv at zero whenever fef_efe​ is continuous, no matter how Z(w)Z(w)Z(w) was chosen. Individuals can shift the location of their score distribution, and thereby their probability of treatment Pr⁡[e≥−Z(w)∣W=w]\Pr[e\geq-Z(w)|W=w]Pr[e≥−Z(w)∣W=w], but they cannot remove the continuity. If eee is absent (complete control), V=Z(w)V=Z(w)V=Z(w) is degenerate, F(0∣w)F(0|w)F(0∣w) is zero or one, and both parts of Condition 2b fail; strategic individuals then bunch just above the threshold. The variance of eee may be arbitrarily small: the identification argument only needs it to be non-zero, although a small variance means that few types receive non-negligible weight f(0∣w)/f(0)f(0|w)/f(0)f(0∣w)/f(0) in equations (10) and (17).

This is the reduced form of the dummy endogenous-variable model of Heckman (1978), the standard parametric selection model, numbered (2) in the paper. The first line is the outcome equation: y1y_1y1​ is the outcome, x1x_1x1​ a vector of exogenous covariates with coefficients α1\alpha_1α1​, ddd the treatment dummy, β\betaβ its (constant) effect, and u1u_1u1​ the error. The second line is the selection equation: y2∗y_2^*y2∗​ is a latent index driven by exogenous variables x2x_2x2​ with coefficients α2\alpha_2α2​ and an error u2u_2u2​. The third line says that treatment is received when the index is non-negative; the paper prints it as two cases, d=1d=1d=1 if y2∗≥0y_2^*\geq0y2∗​≥0 and d=0d=0d=0 if y2∗<0y_2^*<0y2∗​<0.

Selection on unobservables arises because u1u_1u1​ and u2u_2u2​ may be correlated: individuals with a high latent index may have systematically different outcome errors, so E[u1∣d=1]E[u_1|d=1]E[u1​∣d=1] differs from E[u1∣d=0]E[u_1|d=0]E[u1​∣d=0] and OLS of y1y_1y1​ on x1x_1x1​ and ddd is biased. With bivariate normal errors independent of (x1,x2)(x_1,x_2)(x1​,x2​) and Var⁡(u2)\operatorname{Var}(u_2)Var(u2​) normalized to one,

E[u1∣x1,x2,d=1]=Cov⁡(u1,u2) ϕ(x2α2)Φ(x2α2)E[u_1|x_1,x_2,d=1]=\operatorname{Cov}(u_1,u_2)\,\frac{\phi(x_2\alpha_2)}{\Phi(x_2\alpha_2)}E[u1​∣x1​,x2​,d=1]=Cov(u1​,u2​)Φ(x2​α2​)ϕ(x2​α2​)​

where ϕ\phiϕ and Φ\PhiΦ are the standard normal density and cdf; this is the familiar control function. Identification of β\betaβ in this approach rests on the distributional assumption, the independence assumption and an exclusion restriction (x2x_2x2​ contains variables absent from x1x_1x1​). The model is included to show that the regression-discontinuity structure is already present in it: the latent index y2∗y_2^*y2∗​ is a score with threshold zero, as equation (21) makes explicit. The only difference is that here the score is unobserved, and that is what forces the reliance on functional form.

The mapping is obtained by reading equation (20) as a potential-outcomes model. The treatment rule in the third line of equation (20) has the form of equation (7) with the latent index as the score:

d=1[y2∗≥0]⟹V=y2∗,D=dd=1[y_2^*\geq0]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad V=y_2^*,\qquad D=dd=1[y2∗​≥0]⟹V=y2∗​,D=d

The potential outcomes are the values of the outcome equation, the first line of equation (20), when the treatment dummy is set to one and to zero while everything else is held fixed:

Y1=y1∣d=1=x1α1+β+u1,Y0=y1∣d=0=x1α1+u1Y_1=y_1\big|_{d=1}=x_1\alpha_1+\beta+u_1,\qquad Y_0=y_1\big|_{d=0}=x_1\alpha_1+u_1Y1​=y1​​d=1​=x1​α1​+β+u1​,Y0​=y1​​d=0​=x1​α1​+u1​

and the observed outcome is y1=dY1+(1−d)Y0y_1=dY_1+(1-d)Y_0y1​=dY1​+(1−d)Y0​, as in equation (1). The error that appears is necessarily u1u_1u1​, the error of the outcome equation: the model has only the two errors (u1,u2)(u_1,u_2)(u1​,u2​), and the paper's surrounding text refers to "the errors u1,u2u_1,u_2u1​,u2​". The paper's unsubscripted uuu in this sentence is a dropped subscript, and the note's u1u_1u1​ is the consistent reading.

Check of Condition 1b. Take the type to be W=(x1,x2,u1)W=(x_1,x_2,u_1)W=(x1​,x2​,u1​). Then Y1Y_1Y1​ and Y0Y_0Y0​ are functions of WWW alone, and so is any pre-determined variable such as x1x_1x1​.

Check of Condition 2b. Conditional on WWW, the score is V=x2α2+u2V=x_2\alpha_2+u_2V=x2​α2​+u2​ with x2x_2x2​ fixed, so its density is that of u2u_2u2​ given u1u_1u1​, shifted by x2α2x_2\alpha_2x2​α2​. Under bivariate normality with correlation ρ\rhoρ, ∣ρ∣<1|\rho|<1∣ρ∣<1, and unit variances this is a normal density,

V ∣ W ∼ N(x2α2+ρu1, 1−ρ2)V\,|\,W\ \sim\ N\left(x_2\alpha_2+\rho u_1,\ 1-\rho^2\right)V∣W ∼ N(x2​α2​+ρu1​, 1−ρ2)

which is continuous in vvv everywhere and puts positive probability on both sides of zero, so 0<F(0∣w)<10<F(0|w)<10<F(0∣w)<1. Hence Proposition 2 applies. Because Y1−Y0=βY_1-Y_0=\betaY1​−Y0​=β for every type, equation (10) gives ATE∗=βATE^*=\betaATE∗=β whatever the weights: with the index observed, β\betaβ is the jump in E[y1∣y2∗]E[y_1|y_2^*]E[y1​∣y2∗​] at zero, and neither normality nor independence nor the exclusion restriction is needed (any continuous conditional density of u2u_2u2​ would do).

The expression is the regression-discontinuity gap of equation (10) computed for a covariate instead of the outcome. The claim attached to it is that it equals zero under Conditions 1b and 2b. To see this, note that x1x_1x1​ is determined before the latent index is realized, so under the mapping of equation (21) it is a function of the type, x1=x(W)x_1=x(W)x1​=x(W), with the score V=y2∗V=y_2^*V=y2∗​. Its conditional mean at any value vvv of the score is, by equation (12),

E[x1∣y2∗=v]=∫−∞∞x(w) g(w∣v) dw=∫−∞∞x(w)f(v∣w)f(v)g(w) dwE[x_1|y_2^*=v]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(w)\,g(w|v)\,dw=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(w)\frac{f(v|w)}{f(v)}g(w)\,dwE[x1​∣y2∗​=v]=∫−∞∞​x(w)g(w∣v)dw=∫−∞∞​x(w)f(v)f(v∣w)​g(w)dw

Unlike the outcome, x1x_1x1​ is the same function of www on both sides of the threshold: there is no switch from y0y_0y0​ to y1y_1y1​. Taking the limit from the left exactly as in equation (14):

lim⁡Δ→0−E[x1∣y2∗=Δ]=∫−∞∞x(w)f(0∣w)f(0)g(w) dw=E[x1∣y2∗=0]\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E[x_1|y_2^*=\Delta]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(w)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}g(w)\,dw=E[x_1|y_2^*=0]Δ→0−lim​E[x1​∣y2∗​=Δ]=∫−∞∞​x(w)f(0)f(0∣w)​g(w)dw=E[x1​∣y2∗​=0]

Therefore

E[x1∣y2∗=0]−lim⁡Δ→0−E[x1∣y2∗=Δ]=∫−∞∞(x(w)−x(w))f(0∣w)f(0)g(w) dw=0E[x_1|y_2^*=0]-\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E[x_1|y_2^*=\Delta]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(x(w)-x(w)\right)\frac{f(0|w)}{f(0)}g(w)\,dw=0E[x1​∣y2∗​=0]−Δ→0−lim​E[x1​∣y2∗​=Δ]=∫−∞∞​(x(w)−x(w))f(0)f(0∣w)​g(w)dw=0

This is Proposition 2(c), equation (11), applied to the mean of x1x_1x1​. A non-zero estimate of this gap is evidence against Condition 2b: if some types can place themselves precisely above zero, f(v∣w)f(v|w)f(v∣w) jumps at zero for those types, g(w∣v)g(w|v)g(w∣v) is discontinuous, and the mean of any covariate correlated with those types jumps too. The same holds for x2x_2x2​ and for any other pre-determined variable, which is why the covariates are over-identifying checks here and not requirements for identification.

This is the paper's model of two consecutive elections in district iii, numbered (3) there; it also includes the assumption that fi1(v∣w)f_{i1}(v|w)fi1​(v∣w), the density of vi1v_{i1}vi1​ given wi1w_{i1}wi1​, is continuous in vvv. The first line is a causal (structural) equation for the Democratic vote share in year 2: wi1w_{i1}wi1​ collects all characteristics and choices fixed by election day in year 1 (partisan make-up, party resources, candidate quality), with effect α\alphaα; vi1v_{i1}vi1​ is the year-1 Democratic vote share, allowed a direct continuous effect β\betaβ (for example through donors); di2d_{i2}di2​ indicates that the Democrats are the incumbent party in the year-2 race, and γ\gammaγ, the parameter of interest, is the electoral advantage of incumbency; ei2e_{i2}ei2​ is a mean-independent shock. The second line is the deterministic assignment rule: incumbency is won by obtaining at least half of the vote. The third line makes ei2e_{i2}ei2​ unrelated to both year-1 variables.

OLS of vi2v_{i2}vi2​ on vi1v_{i1}vi1​ and di2d_{i2}di2​ is inconsistent because elements of wi1w_{i1}wi1​ are unobserved and correlated with vi1v_{i1}vi1​, hence with di2d_{i2}di2​. No instrument or control strategy is proposed. Identification of γ\gammaγ comes from the discontinuity alone:

E[vi2∣vi1=v]=αE[wi1∣vi1=v]+βv+γ⋅1[v≥12]E[v_{i2}|v_{i1}=v]=\alpha E[w_{i1}|v_{i1}=v]+\beta v+\gamma\cdot1\left[v\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\right]E[vi2​∣vi1​=v]=αE[wi1​∣vi1​=v]+βv+γ⋅1[v≥21​]

The first two terms are continuous in vvv at one half (the first by Proposition 3(a), given the continuous density), so the only jump is γ\gammaγ. The variation used is the as-good-as-random outcome of elections decided by very small margins. Linearity and the constant γ\gammaγ are for exposition; equation (24) shows the model is a special case of Condition 1c, and Proposition 3 delivers a weighted average of district-specific gaps when the effect is heterogeneous. Note that β\betaβ here is the direct effect of the lagged vote share, whereas in Appendix B (equations (26) and (27)) the paper uses β\betaβ for the discontinuity gap itself.

The first part is a relabelling of equation (23): set W=wi1W=w_{i1}W=wi1​, V=vi1V=v_{i1}V=vi1​, substitute the assignment rule di2=1[vi1≥12]d_{i2}=1[v_{i1}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}]di2​=1[vi1​≥21​] into the first line, and call the systematic part YYY:

y(w,v)=αw+βv+γ⋅1[v≥12]y(w,v)=\alpha w+\beta v+\gamma\cdot1\left[v\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\right]y(w,v)=αw+βv+γ⋅1[v≥21​]

This function is continuous in vvv except at v=12v=\tfrac{1}{2}v=21​, where the indicator switches on and the function is continuous from the right, as Condition 1c requires (with the threshold at one half instead of zero; replace VVV by V−12V-\tfrac{1}{2}V−21​ to match equation (15) literally). The second part computes the individual gap of equation (16). At the threshold the indicator equals one:

y(w,12)=αw+12β+γy\left(w,\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=\alpha w+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta+\gammay(w,21​)=αw+21​β+γ

Just below the threshold, for ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, the indicator equals zero:

y(w,12−ε)=αw+β(12−ε) ⟶ αw+12βas ε→0+y\left(w,\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon\right)=\alpha w+\beta\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon\right)\ \longrightarrow\ \alpha w+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\to0^+y(w,21​−ε)=αw+β(21​−ε) ⟶ αw+21​βas ε→0+

Subtracting, the type term and the direct effect of the vote share cancel:

y(w,12)−lim⁡ε→0+y(w,12−ε)=(αw+12β+γ)−(αw+12β)=γy\left(w,\tfrac{1}{2}\right)-\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}y\left(w,\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon\right)=\left(\alpha w+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta+\gamma\right)-\left(\alpha w+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta\right)=\gammay(w,21​)−ε→0+lim​y(w,21​−ε)=(αw+21​β+γ)−(αw+21​β)=γ

So y+(w)−y−(w)=γy^+(w)-y^-(w)=\gammay+(w)−y−(w)=γ for every www. Plugging this constant gap into equation (17) and using the fact that the weights integrate to one,

ATE∗∗=∫−∞∞γ f(12∣w)f(12) dG(w)=γATE^{**}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\gamma\,\frac{f(\tfrac{1}{2}|w)}{f(\tfrac{1}{2})}\,dG(w)=\gammaATE∗∗=∫−∞∞​γf(21​)f(21​∣w)​dG(w)=γ

so the regression-discontinuity gap identifies γ\gammaγ exactly in this model, without observing wi1w_{i1}wi1​ and without knowing α\alphaα or β\betaβ.

The observed outcome differs from the response function of equation (24) by the error: from the first line of equation (23), vi2=Y+ei2v_{i2}=Y+e_{i2}vi2​=Y+ei2​ with Y=y(wi1,vi1)Y=y(w_{i1},v_{i1})Y=y(wi1​,vi1​). Take expectations conditional on the year-1 vote share:

E[vi2∣vi1]=E[Y∣vi1]+E[ei2∣vi1]E[v_{i2}|v_{i1}]=E[Y|v_{i1}]+E[e_{i2}|v_{i1}]E[vi2​∣vi1​]=E[Y∣vi1​]+E[ei2​∣vi1​]

The last term is zero by the law of iterated expectations and the third line of equation (23): conditioning on vi1v_{i1}vi1​ alone is coarser than conditioning on (wi1,vi1)(w_{i1},v_{i1})(wi1​,vi1​), so

E[ei2∣vi1]=E[ E[ei2∣wi1,vi1] ∣ vi1]=E[0 ∣ vi1]=0E[e_{i2}|v_{i1}]=E\left[\,E[e_{i2}|w_{i1},v_{i1}]\ \big|\ v_{i1}\right]=E[0\,|\,v_{i1}]=0E[ei2​∣vi1​]=E[E[ei2​∣wi1​,vi1​] ​ vi1​]=E[0∣vi1​]=0

Hence E[vi2∣vi1]=E[Y∣vi1]E[v_{i2}|v_{i1}]=E[Y|v_{i1}]E[vi2​∣vi1​]=E[Y∣vi1​], which is equation (25). This is the paper's footnote 13, the "trivial modification" needed because Condition 1c, equation (15), has no error term. The consequence is that the observable conditional mean of the year-2 vote share has the same discontinuity as the conditional mean of YYY, to which Proposition 3 applies:

E[vi2∣vi1=12]−lim⁡Δ→0−E[vi2∣vi1=12+Δ]=ATE∗∗=γE\left[v_{i2}|v_{i1}=\tfrac{1}{2}\right]-\lim_{\Delta\to0^-}E\left[v_{i2}|v_{i1}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\Delta\right]=ATE^{**}=\gammaE[vi2​∣vi1​=21​]−Δ→0−lim​E[vi2​∣vi1​=21​+Δ]=ATE∗∗=γ

using equations (17) and (24). The mean-independence assumption matters only at this step: the shock realized after election 1 must not be systematically different for barely-winning and barely-losing districts. An error with E[ei2∣wi1,vi1]E[e_{i2}|w_{i1},v_{i1}]E[ei2​∣wi1​,vi1​] non-zero but continuous in vi1v_{i1}vi1​ at one half could simply be absorbed into y(w,v)y(w,v)y(w,v) and would leave the result unchanged.

The sophomore surge is one of three traditional measures of the incumbent legislator advantage that Appendix B contrasts with the regression-discontinuity estimate; the formula is the label printed in panel (a) of the paper's Fig. B1. The sample is districts won in period 1 by a Democrat running as a non-incumbent (a freshman). V2‾\overline{V_2}V2​​ is the average Democratic vote share of these legislators in period 2, when they run as incumbents for the first time, and V1‾\overline{V_1}V1​​ is the average share the same people obtained in period 1, when they first won. Both are vote shares between zero and one, and the surge is expected to be positive. In the figure the pair (V1‾,V2‾)(\overline{V_1},\overline{V_2})(V1​​,V2​​) is a single point on the dotted line for freshman Democrats, to the right of 0.5.

The logic is a before-after comparison for the same candidate in the same district: V1‾\overline{V_1}V1​​ is taken as a measure of the strength of the party in those districts apart from any incumbency advantage, so the gain is attributed to being the incumbent legislator. For example, an average of 0.56 as first-time winners and 0.62 two years later gives a surge of 0.06. The comparison is not the paper's estimand. The regression-discontinuity gap is a vertical jump at V1=0.5V_1=0.5V1​=0.5 between districts on the two sides of the threshold, the incumbent party advantage γ\gammaγ of equation (23), which Appendix B calls β\betaβ. The surge instead compares two periods within the winning side, conditions on having won (a sample selected on a high realization of V1V_1V1​) and on running again, and need not bear any relation to the gap: either can be zero while the other is large.

The retirement slump is the mirror image of the sophomore surge of equation (26); the expression is the label in panel (b) of the paper's Fig. B1 (the figure prints the label and the difference side by side, without an equality sign). The sample is now districts held by a Democratic incumbent who retires, so that the seat is open in period 2. Here V1‾\overline{V_1}V1​​ is the average Democratic share won by the retiring incumbents in their last election, and V2‾\overline{V_2}V2​​ is the average share won by the new Democratic candidates in the same districts in period 2. The bars denote averages over this open-seat sample, not over the freshman sample of equation (26), and the order of subtraction is reversed so that a positive number again measures an advantage: the votes the party loses when the incumbent legislator is replaced by a newcomer. In the figure the point (V1‾,V2‾)(\overline{V_1},\overline{V_2})(V1​​,V2​​) lies on the dashed line for seats open in period 2.

The measure treats the incoming candidate's share as the strength of the party without an incumbent legislator. For example, retiring incumbents averaging 0.68 followed by successors averaging 0.60 give a slump of 0.08. Like the surge, it is a within-district comparison over time on one side of the threshold and requires that seats be thrown open, and retirement is itself a choice. The Gelman-King index ψ\psiψ in the same panel is the vertical distance between the line for seats with an incumbent running and the parallel line for open seats, holding V1V_1V1​ fixed. All three measure an incumbent legislator advantage; the regression-discontinuity gap at 0.5, the γ\gammaγ of equation (23), measures the incumbent party advantage and is logically unrelated to them.
